title: How do you enforce least privilege at the Pod level — `securityContext` with `runAsNonRoot`/`runAsUser`, `readOnlyRootFilesystem`, dropped Linux capabilities, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, and cluster-wide Pod Security Standards/admission (restricted profile) — and why does a container running as root breach "least privilege"?
shortTitle: Enforcing Least Privilege at the Pod Level and Why Running as Root Breaches It

s1_definition.profdef: Least privilege at the Pod level means a container runs with only the permissions it truly needs and nothing more. You enforce it with a securityContext that sets runAsNonRoot and a specific non-zero runAsUser, mounts the root filesystem read-only, drops all Linux capabilities and adds back only the few that are required, and sets allowPrivilegeEscalation to false so a process cannot gain more privileges than it started with. Cluster-wide, Pod Security Admission enforces these rules at admission time using the restricted profile, so non-compliant Pods are rejected. A container running as root breaches least privilege because the root user inside the container maps to a powerful identity that, combined with a kernel or runtime vulnerability, can escalate to control the node.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, least privilege means a junior clerk gets a key that opens only their own drawer, not the vault, the server room, and the CEO's office. The securityContext is the access-control form that says exactly which single drawer this clerk may open, forbids them from carrying tools that pick other locks, and bans them from upgrading their own badge. Pod Security Admission is the security desk at the entrance that refuses to let anyone in who demands master keys. Running as root is like handing every new clerk the building master key on day one, so if any one of them is compromised the attacker owns the whole building.
s1_definition.oneliner: Give a container only the permissions it needs via securityContext, enforce it cluster-wide with the restricted Pod Security profile, and never run as root because root plus one exploit means node takeover.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Least privilege at the Pod level means a container runs with only the permissions it truly needs and nothing more. You enforce it with a securityContext that sets runAsNonRoot and a specific non-zero runAsUser, mounts the root filesystem read-only, drops all Linux capabilities and adds back only the few that are required, and sets allowPrivilegeEscalation to false so a process cannot gain more privileges than it started with. Cluster-wide, Pod Security Admission enforces these rules at admission time using the restricted profile, so non-compliant Pods are rejected. A container running as root breaches least privilege because the root user inside the container maps to a powerful identity that, combined with a kernel or runtime vulnerability, can escalate to control the node.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, least privilege means a junior clerk gets a key that opens only their own drawer, not the vault, the server room, and the CEO's office. The securityContext is the access-control form that says exactly which single drawer this clerk may open, forbids them from carrying tools that pick other locks, and bans them from upgrading their own badge. Pod Security Admission is the security desk at the entrance that refuses to let anyone in who demands master keys. Running as root is like handing every new clerk the building master key on day one, so if any one of them is compromised the attacker owns the whole building.

**One line to remember:** Give a container only the permissions it needs via securityContext, enforce it cluster-wide with the restricted Pod Security profile, and never run as root because root plus one exploit means node takeover.

sections.s2_technical:
The securityContext is set at the Pod level and can be overridden per container, and several fields together implement least privilege. `runAsNonRoot: true` makes the kubelet refuse to start a container whose image would run as UID 0, which is a safety net. `runAsUser` with a specific non-zero UID, such as 10001, pins the process to an unprivileged account. `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` makes the container's root filesystem immutable, so an attacker cannot drop a malicious binary or tamper with code; the application writes only to explicitly mounted writable volumes like an emptyDir for temporary files.

Linux capabilities are a finer-grained split of root's powers. By default containers get a set of capabilities even as non-root, and least privilege means dropping all of them with `capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]` and adding back only the specific ones a workload genuinely needs, which for a typical banking microservice is none. `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` sets the no-new-privileges flag so a child process cannot gain more privileges than its parent, which blocks setuid-based escalation. Together these shrink the blast radius: even if the application is compromised, the attacker is a non-root user on a read-only filesystem with no capabilities and no way to escalate.

Enforcing this per Pod is good, but relying on every team to remember it is fragile, so Kubernetes provides Pod Security Admission built into the API server. It defines three profiles: privileged (no restrictions), baseline (blocks known privilege escalations), and restricted (the hardened profile that requires runAsNonRoot, dropped capabilities, no privilege escalation, and a restricted seccomp profile). You label a namespace with the profile and a mode: enforce rejects violating Pods, audit records them, and warn returns a warning. For a banking namespace I enforce the restricted profile so any Pod that tries to run as root or request extra capabilities is rejected at admission time, before it ever runs. Many teams layer a policy engine like OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno on top for custom rules such as requiring specific labels or forbidding certain registries.

Why does running as root breach least privilege even inside a container? A container is not a strong security boundary like a virtual machine; it shares the host kernel. Root inside the container is, by default, the same UID 0 the kernel recognizes, so if an attacker escapes the container through a kernel bug, a misconfigured mount, or an added capability like CAP_SYS_ADMIN, they are root on the node and can read every other Pod's secrets, mounted volumes, and the kubelet credentials. Running as an unprivileged user with dropped capabilities and no escalation means that even a successful application compromise is contained to a weak identity that cannot pivot to the node. In a bank, where one node runs many tenants' Pods, that containment is the difference between a single compromised service and a cluster-wide breach.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India a security review of our Transfer Service drove this hardening. Two concrete problems motivated it.

Problem 1 — the base image ran the app as root and the root filesystem was writable, so a code-injection bug could have let an attacker write a malicious binary and, with the default capabilities, probe for a container escape to the node. This is exactly why we set runAsNonRoot, a fixed UID, a read-only root filesystem, dropped all capabilities, and disabled privilege escalation.

Problem 2 — nothing stopped a new team from shipping a Pod that ran as root, so the protection was only as strong as the least careful team. This is exactly why we labelled the namespace with the restricted Pod Security profile in enforce mode, so a root Pod is rejected at admission.

The mini-project is a runnable Java simulation of a `PodSecurityContext` holding the hardening fields, a `PodSecurityAdmission` that applies the restricted profile and admits or rejects a Pod, and a `BlastRadius` estimator that shows how much an attacker could reach with a root versus a hardened Pod. We admit a hardened Transfer Service that then serves Rajesh and Priya, and reject a root Pod.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile and run the pod security simulation
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/sec/*.java
java -cp out com.bank.sec.PodSecurityDemo

# Real cluster: label namespace and watch a root Pod get rejected
kubectl label ns banking-prod pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted
kubectl -n banking-prod run root-test --image=busybox --command -- sleep 1d  # rejected
kubectl get pod transfer-xyz -o jsonpath='{.spec.securityContext}'           # verify hardening
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: one Pod using the insecure defaults (root) and one hardened Pod, both submitted to a namespace enforcing the restricted profile.

Step 1 — The blast-radius estimator looks at the root Pod. It runs as UID 0, allows privilege escalation, and keeps all capabilities, so the estimator reports a HIGH blast radius: a compromise could escape the container and take over the node and every other Pod's secrets.

Step 2 — Admission evaluates the root Pod against the restricted profile. It collects violations: not runAsNonRoot, writable root filesystem, privilege escalation allowed, capabilities not dropped, and an unconfined seccomp profile. Because the list is non-empty, the Pod is rejected before it ever runs.

Step 3 — The blast-radius estimator looks at the hardened Pod. It runs as UID 10001, forbids escalation, and drops all capabilities, so the estimator reports a LOW blast radius: even a full application compromise is contained to a weak identity on a read-only filesystem.

Step 4 — Admission evaluates the hardened Pod. Every requirement is satisfied, so the Pod is admitted.

Step 5 — Because the hardened Pod is admitted and runs, a transfer of fifty thousand rupees from Rajesh to Priya executes successfully, proving that strong least-privilege settings do not prevent the application from doing its real job.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 01:02:20.100 [SEVERE] blast radius: HIGH — root + caps + escalation -> container escape -> NODE takeover -> all Pods' secrets
2026-10-30 01:02:20.101 [SEVERE] REJECT transfer-root — restricted profile violations: [must runAsNonRoot (non-zero UID), root filesystem must be read-only, allowPrivilegeEscalation must be false, must drop ALL capabilities (added=[ALL]), seccomp must be RuntimeDefault]
2026-10-30 01:02:20.102 [INFO] blast radius: LOW — unprivileged UID, read-only FS, no caps, no escalation -> contained to this app
2026-10-30 01:02:20.103 [INFO] ADMIT transfer-hardened (restricted profile satisfied)
2026-10-30 01:02:20.104 [INFO] transfer SAV2001->CUR3001 Rs.50000 SUCCESS on hardened pod (UID 10001, RO FS, no caps)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Least privilege at the Pod level means a container runs with only the permissions it genuinely needs and nothing more, and I implement it through the securityContext. I set runAsNonRoot to true and pin a specific non-zero user ID so the process never runs as root. I mount the root filesystem read-only so an attacker cannot drop a malicious binary or tamper with code, and I give the application a small writable volume only where it truly needs to write. I drop all Linux capabilities and add back only the handful a workload actually requires, which for a typical banking microservice is none. And I set allowPrivilegeEscalation to false so a child process can never gain more privileges than its parent, which blocks setuid-based escalation.

Doing this per Pod is necessary but not sufficient, because relying on every team to remember it is fragile. So cluster-wide I use Pod Security Admission, which is built into the API server and offers privileged, baseline, and restricted profiles. I label the banking namespace with the restricted profile in enforce mode, so any Pod that tries to run as root, keep extra capabilities, or allow escalation is rejected at admission time before it ever runs. For custom organizational rules I layer a policy engine like Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper on top.

The reason running as root breaches least privilege, even inside a container, is that a container is not a strong security boundary the way a virtual machine is; it shares the host kernel. Root inside the container is, by default, the same privileged identity the kernel recognizes, so if an attacker escapes the container through a kernel bug, a bad mount, or a dangerous capability, they become root on the node and can read every other Pod's secrets, mounted volumes, and the node's credentials. Running as an unprivileged user with dropped capabilities and no escalation means that even a full application compromise is contained to a weak identity that cannot pivot to the node.

In my project at the National Bank of India a security review found our Transfer Service running as root with a writable filesystem, which meant a single code-injection bug could have led to a node takeover. We hardened it to run as a fixed unprivileged user on a read-only filesystem with all capabilities dropped and escalation disabled, and crucially we labelled the namespace with the restricted profile in enforce mode so no team could ever ship a root Pod again. The service kept doing its job of moving customers' money exactly as before, but the blast radius of any compromise shrank from the entire cluster to a single weak, contained process, which in a multi-tenant banking cluster is the whole point.

keyPoints: Pod: smallest deployable unit, one or more containers
Deployment: declarative pod management with replica count
Service: stable network endpoint for a set of pods
